cues.text: A Mother's Tears and a Son's Ambition

Born in 354 at Tagaste in Roman North Africa to a pagan father and a devoutly Christian mother, Monica , Augustine received an excellent classical education that his family sacrificed considerably to afford.
He showed from a young age both a brilliant intellect and a restless, ambitious temperament.
That temperament carried him, in his teens and twenties, into a live-in relationship with a mistress and the birth of a son he named Adeodatus.
More troubling still to his mother, it also carried him into membership in the Manichaean sect.

Its dualistic explanation of good and evil offered the young Augustine an intellectually satisfying, if ultimately false, answer to questions Christianity's simpler teaching had not yet managed to satisfy for him.

Throughout these years of wandering, his mother's response, as Augustine himself would later record with unforgettable tenderness, was neither despair nor rejection but an unbroken campaign of tears and prayer that followed him, quite literally, across the sea.
A Teacher Drawn to Milan
Augustine's brilliant rhetorical gifts carried him from Carthage to Rome and finally, in 384, to Milan , where he took up a prestigious position teaching rhetoric at the imperial court.
There he came, at first purely to study the older man's celebrated eloquence, under the preaching of the city's formidable bishop, Ambrose .

Over many months, almost against his own will, Augustine found Ambrose's careful, intellectually serious explanation of Scripture dismantling, one by one, the objections to Christianity he had nursed for years.
All the while, his own inner life grew more and more divided.
On one hand was the pull of a worldly career and marriage.
On the other was an increasingly undeniable summons to a different kind of life.
A Voice in the Garden
The crisis broke in a garden in Milan in the late summer of 386.
Augustine, in an agony of indecision over his own divided will, heard what seemed to be a child's voice from a neighboring house repeating the words tolle, lege — "take up and read."
Taking this as a divine instruction, he opened at random a book of St. Paul's letters lying nearby.
His eyes fell immediately on a passage from Romans urging its readers to put aside sensuality and clothe themselves instead in Christ.

Augustine describes the effect as instantaneous and total: every remaining shadow of doubt and hesitation, he tells us, was in that moment simply dispelled, and he resolved then and there to give himself entirely and finally to Christ.
He was baptized by Ambrose himself the following Easter, his mother Monica present at the font to see, at last, the answer to seventeen years of prayer.
Bishop of Hippo
Returning to North Africa after his mother's death, Augustine was, almost against his own wishes, ordained a priest and then, in 395 or 396, made bishop of the small coastal town of Hippo Regius .
He would govern that see for the following thirty-five years with an energy that belied its modest size.

He preached constantly, resolved disputes among his own flock with tireless patience, and engaged, through an enormous body of letters and treatises, virtually every major theological controversy of his age.
Against the Manichaeans who had once held him, he defended the goodness of the created world and the reality of free will.
Against the Donatists who divided the African Church over the worthiness of its ministers, he defended the unity and universal reach of the one Church.
Pelagius, a British monk, taught that human beings could achieve their own salvation by unaided moral effort.
Against him, Augustine defended, with unmatched theological depth, the absolute necessity of God's grace for any good work whatsoever.
A Life Laid Bare, and a City of God

Around 397, at the urging of friends, Augustine wrote his Confessions , an extended prayer addressed directly to God recounting his own conversion with a psychological candor no ancient writer, pagan or Christian, had ever before attempted.
It remains, sixteen centuries later, one of the most read and most personally moving books in the entire history of Christian literature.
When Rome itself fell to the Goths in 410, pagan critics blamed the disaster on the empire's abandonment of the old gods for Christianity.
Augustine responded with his other great masterwork, The City of God , a sweeping theological account of human history as the intertwined but ultimately distinct story of two cities.
One was built on love of self, the other on love of God.
It would shape Western political and theological thought for the rest of the Middle Ages and beyond.
Legacy
Augustine died at Hippo in August 430, as Vandal armies laid siege to the very city he had shepherded for over three decades, the wider Roman world of his youth already visibly crumbling around him.
Few theologians in the entire history of the Church have shaped Western Christian thought as decisively or as lastingly as this once-restless, once-wandering son of Monica's endless prayers.
He shaped it on grace, sin, the sacraments, the nature of time, and the relationship between faith and reason.

His own most famous words remain, for every human heart that has ever felt itself divided and searching, simply and permanently true: Thou hast made us for Thyself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in Thee .
